name: workers-best-practices
description: Reviews and authors Cloudflare Workers code against production best practices. Load when writing new Workers, reviewing Worker code, configuring wrangler.jsonc, or checking for common Workers anti-patterns (streaming, floating promises, global state, secrets, bindings, observability). Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
---

Your knowledge of Cloudflare Workers APIs, types, and configuration may be outdated. **Prefer retrieval over pre-training** for any Workers code task — writing or reviewing.

## Retrieval Sources

Fetch the **latest** versions before writing or reviewing Workers code. Do not rely on baked-in knowledge for API signatures, config fields, or binding shapes.

| Source | How to retrieve | Use for |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| Workers best practices | Fetch `https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/best-practices/workers-best-practices/` | Canonical rules, patterns, anti-patterns |
| Workers types | See `references/review.md` for retrieval steps | API signatures, handler types, binding types |
| Wrangler config schema | `node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json` | Config fields, binding shapes, allowed values |
| Cloudflare docs | Search tool or `https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/` | API reference, compatibility dates/flags |

## FIRST: Fetch Latest References

Before reviewing or writing Workers code, retrieve the current best practices page and relevant type definitions. If the project's `node_modules` has an older version, **prefer the latest published version**.

```bash
# Fetch latest workers types
mkdir -p /tmp/workers-types-latest && \
  npm pack @cloudflare/workers-types --pack-destination /tmp/workers-types-latest && \
  tar -xzf /tmp/workers-types-latest/cloudflare-workers-types-*.tgz -C /tmp/workers-types-latest
# Types at /tmp/workers-types-latest/package/index.d.ts
```

## Reference Documentation

- `references/rules.md` — all best practice rules with code examples and anti-patterns
- `references/review.md` — type validation, config validation, binding access patterns, review process

## Rules Quick Reference

### Configuration

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Compatibility date | Set `compatibility_date` to today on new projects; update periodically on existing ones |
| nodejs_compat | Enable the `nodejs_compat` flag — many libraries depend on Node.js built-ins |
| wrangler types | Run `wrangler types` to generate `Env` — never hand-write binding interfaces |
| Secrets | Use `wrangler secret put`, never hardcode secrets in config or source |
| wrangler.jsonc | Use JSONC config for non-secret settings — newer features are JSON-only |

### Request & Response Handling

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Streaming | Stream large/unknown payloads — never `await response.text()` on unbounded data |
| waitUntil | Use `ctx.waitUntil()` for post-response work; do not destructure `ctx` |

### Architecture

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Bindings over REST | Use in-process bindings (KV, R2, D1, Queues) — not the Cloudflare REST API |
| Queues & Workflows | Move async/background work off the critical path |
| Service bindings | Use service bindings for Worker-to-Worker calls — not public HTTP |
| Hyperdrive | Always use Hyperdrive for external PostgreSQL/MySQL connections |

### Observability

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Logs & Traces | Enable `observability` in config with `head_sampling_rate`; use structured JSON logging |

### Code Patterns

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| No global request state | Never store request-scoped data in module-level variables |
| Floating promises | Every Promise must be `await`ed, `return`ed, `void`ed, or passed to `ctx.waitUntil()` |

### Security

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Web Crypto | Use `crypto.randomUUID()` / `crypto.getRandomValues()` — never `Math.random()` for security |
| No passThroughOnException | Use explicit try/catch with structured error responses |

## Anti-Patterns to Flag

| Anti-pattern | Why it matters |
|-------------|----------------|
| `await response.text()` on unbounded data | Memory exhaustion — 128 MB limit |
| Hardcoded secrets in source or config | Credential leak via version control |
| `Math.random()` for tokens/IDs | Predictable, not cryptographically secure |
| Bare `fetch()` without `await` or `waitUntil` | Floating promise — dropped result, swallowed error |
| Module-level mutable variables for request state | Cross-request data leaks, stale state, I/O errors |
| Cloudflare REST API from inside a Worker | Unnecessary network hop, auth overhead, added latency |
| `ctx.passThroughOnException()` as error handling | Hides bugs, makes debugging impossible |
| Hand-written `Env` interface | Drifts from actual wrangler config bindings |
| Direct string comparison for secret values | Timing side-channel — use `crypto.subtle.timingSafeEqual` |
| Destructuring `ctx` (`const { waitUntil } = ctx`) | Loses `this` binding — throws "Illegal invocation" at runtime |
| `any` on `Env` or handler params | Defeats type safety for all binding access |
| `as unknown as T` double-cast | Hides real type incompatibilities — fix the design |
| `implements` on platform base classes (instead of `extends`) | Legacy — loses `this.ctx`, `this.env`. Applies to DurableObject, WorkerEntrypoint, Workflow |
| `env.X` inside platform base class | Should be `this.env.X` in classes extending DurableObject, WorkerEntrypoint, etc. |

## Review Workflow

1. **Retrieve** — fetch latest best practices page, workers types, and wrangler schema
2. **Read full files** — not just diffs; context matters for binding access patterns
3. **Check types** — binding access, handler signatures, no `any`, no unsafe casts (see `references/review.md`)
4. **Check config** — compatibility_date, nodejs_compat, observability, secrets, binding-code consistency
5. **Check patterns** — streaming, floating promises, global state, serialization boundaries
6. **Check security** — crypto usage, secret handling, timing-safe comparisons, error handling
7. **Validate with tools** — `npx tsc --noEmit`, lint for `no-floating-promises`
8. **Reference rules** — see `references/rules.md` for each rule's correct pattern

## Scope

This skill covers Workers-specific best practices and code review. For related topics:

- **Durable Objects**: load the `durable-objects` skill
- **Workflows**: see [Rules of Workflows](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/rules-of-workflows/)
- **Wrangler CLI commands**: load the `wrangler` skill

## Principles

- **Be certain.** Retrieve before flagging. If unsure about an API, config field, or pattern, fetch the docs first.
- **Provide evidence.** Reference line numbers, tool output, or docs links.
- **Focus on what developers will copy.** Workers code in examples and docs gets pasted into production.
- **Correctness over completeness.** A concise example that works beats a comprehensive one with errors.

# Cloudflare Platform Skill

Consolidated skill for building on the Cloudflare platform. Use decision trees below to find the right product, then load detailed references.

Your knowledge of Cloudflare APIs, types, limits, and pricing may be outdated. **Prefer retrieval over pre-training** — the references in this skill are starting points, not source of truth.

## Retrieval Sources

Fetch the **latest** information before citing specific numbers, API signatures, or configuration options. Do not rely on baked-in knowledge or these reference files alone.

| Wrangler config schema | `node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json` | Config fields, binding shapes, allowed values |
| Product changelogs | `https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/` | Recent changes to limits, features, deprecations |

When a reference file and the docs disagree, **trust the docs**. This is especially important for: numeric limits, pricing tiers, type signatures, and configuration options.

## Quick Decision Trees

### "I need feature flags"

```
Need feature flags?
└─ Feature toggles, targeting rules, percentage rollouts → flagship/

```

### "I need to run code"


name: workers-best-practices
description: Reviews and authors Cloudflare Workers code against production best practices. Load when writing new Workers, reviewing Worker code, configuring wrangler.jsonc, or checking for common Workers anti-patterns (streaming, floating promises, global state, secrets, bindings, observability). Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge.
---

Your knowledge of Cloudflare Workers APIs, types, and configuration may be outdated. **Prefer retrieval over pre-training** for any Workers code task — writing or reviewing.

## Retrieval Sources

Fetch the **latest** versions before writing or reviewing Workers code. Do not rely on baked-in knowledge for API signatures, config fields, or binding shapes.

| Source | How to retrieve | Use for |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| Workers best practices | Fetch `https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/best-practices/workers-best-practices/` | Canonical rules, patterns, anti-patterns |
| Workers types | See `references/review.md` for retrieval steps | API signatures, handler types, binding types |
| Wrangler config schema | `node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json` | Config fields, binding shapes, allowed values |
| Cloudflare docs | Search tool or `https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/` | API reference, compatibility dates/flags |

## FIRST: Fetch Latest References

Before reviewing or writing Workers code, retrieve the current best practices page and relevant type definitions. If the project's `node_modules` has an older version, **prefer the latest published version**.

```bash
# Fetch latest workers types
mkdir -p /tmp/workers-types-latest && \
  npm pack @cloudflare/workers-types --pack-destination /tmp/workers-types-latest && \
  tar -xzf /tmp/workers-types-latest/cloudflare-workers-types-*.tgz -C /tmp/workers-types-latest
# Types at /tmp/workers-types-latest/package/index.d.ts
```

## Reference Documentation

- `references/rules.md` — all best practice rules with code examples and anti-patterns
- `references/review.md` — type validation, config validation, binding access patterns, review process

## Rules Quick Reference

### Configuration

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Compatibility date | Set `compatibility_date` to today on new projects; update periodically on existing ones |
| nodejs_compat | Enable the `nodejs_compat` flag — many libraries depend on Node.js built-ins |
| wrangler types | Run `wrangler types` to generate `Env` — never hand-write binding interfaces |
| Secrets | Use `wrangler secret put`, never hardcode secrets in config or source |
| wrangler.jsonc | Use JSONC config for non-secret settings — newer features are JSON-only |

### Request & Response Handling

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Streaming | Stream large/unknown payloads — never `await response.text()` on unbounded data |
| waitUntil | Use `ctx.waitUntil()` for post-response work; do not destructure `ctx` |

### Architecture

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Bindings over REST | Use in-process bindings (KV, R2, D1, Queues) — not the Cloudflare REST API |
| Queues & Workflows | Move async/background work off the critical path |
| Service bindings | Use service bindings for Worker-to-Worker calls — not public HTTP |
| Hyperdrive | Always use Hyperdrive for external PostgreSQL/MySQL connections |

### Observability

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Logs & Traces | Enable `observability` in config with `head_sampling_rate`; use structured JSON logging |

### Code Patterns

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| No global request state | Never store request-scoped data in module-level variables |
| Floating promises | Every Promise must be `await`ed, `return`ed, `void`ed, or passed to `ctx.waitUntil()` |

### Security

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Web Crypto | Use `crypto.randomUUID()` / `crypto.getRandomValues()` — never `Math.random()` for security |
| No passThroughOnException | Use explicit try/catch with structured error responses |

## Anti-Patterns to Flag

| Anti-pattern | Why it matters |
|-------------|----------------|
| `await response.text()` on unbounded data | Memory exhaustion — 128 MB limit |
| Hardcoded secrets in source or config | Credential leak via version control |
| `Math.random()` for tokens/IDs | Predictable, not cryptographically secure |
| Bare `fetch()` without `await` or `waitUntil` | Floating promise — dropped result, swallowed error |
| Module-level mutable variables for request state | Cross-request data leaks, stale state, I/O errors |
| Cloudflare REST API from inside a Worker | Unnecessary network hop, auth overhead, added latency |
| `ctx.passThroughOnException()` as error handling | Hides bugs, makes debugging impossible |
| Hand-written `Env` interface | Drifts from actual wrangler config bindings |
| Direct string comparison for secret values | Timing side-channel — use `crypto.subtle.timingSafeEqual` |
| Destructuring `ctx` (`const { waitUntil } = ctx`) | Loses `this` binding — throws "Illegal invocation" at runtime |
| `any` on `Env` or handler params | Defeats type safety for all binding access |
| `as unknown as T` double-cast | Hides real type incompatibilities — fix the design |
| `implements` on platform base classes (instead of `extends`) | Legacy — loses `this.ctx`, `this.env`. Applies to DurableObject, WorkerEntrypoint, Workflow |
| `env.X` inside platform base class | Should be `this.env.X` in classes extending DurableObject, WorkerEntrypoint, etc. |

## Review Workflow

1. **Retrieve** — fetch latest best practices page, workers types, and wrangler schema
2. **Read full files** — not just diffs; context matters for binding access patterns
3. **Check types** — binding access, handler signatures, no `any`, no unsafe casts (see `references/review.md`)
4. **Check config** — compatibility_date, nodejs_compat, observability, secrets, binding-code consistency
5. **Check patterns** — streaming, floating promises, global state, serialization boundaries
6. **Check security** — crypto usage, secret handling, timing-safe comparisons, error handling
7. **Validate with tools** — `npx tsc --noEmit`, lint for `no-floating-promises`
8. **Reference rules** — see `references/rules.md` for each rule's correct pattern

## Scope

This skill covers Workers-specific best practices and code review. For related topics:

- **Durable Objects**: load the `durable-objects` skill
- **Workflows**: see [Rules of Workflows](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/rules-of-workflows/)
- **Wrangler CLI commands**: load the `wrangler` skill

## Principles

- **Be certain.** Retrieve before flagging. If unsure about an API, config field, or pattern, fetch the docs first.
- **Provide evidence.** Reference line numbers, tool output, or docs links.
- **Focus on what developers will copy.** Workers code in examples and docs gets pasted into production.
- **Correctness over completeness.** A concise example that works beats a comprehensive one with errors.

L121: ## Introduction
L122: 
L123: The Overpass API (formerly known as OSM Server Side Scripting, or OSM3S before 2011) is a read-only API that serves up custom selected parts of the OSM map data. It acts as a database over the web: the client sends a query to the API and gets back the data set that corresponds to the query.
L124: Unlike the main cite129†API , which is optimized for editing, Overpass API is optimized for data consumers that need a few elements within a glimpse or up to roughly 10 million elements in some minutes, both selected by search criteria like e.g. location, type of objects, tag properties, proximity, or combinations of them. It acts as a database backend for cite109†various services .
L125: 
L126: Please see the cite130†full user's manual†dev.overpass-api.de for a detailed introduction.
L127: There exists in addition a cite92†Overpass QL guide/language reference . It is highly recommended to get familiar with various features via cite111†overpass turbo , an cite131†interactive Web-based frontend†overpass-turbo.eu . For legacy applications, there's also a cite132†compatibility layer to allow a smooth transition from cite133†XAPI .
L128: ## Quick Start (60 seconds): Interactive UI
L129: 
L130: (If interested in raw data see Quick Start: for Developers/Programmers below)
L131:   * Open cite131†overpass turbo†overpass-turbo.eu in a new tab
L132:   * Click on the "Wizard" button
L133:   * Type something like "Drinking Water in London" in the text box
L134:   * Click "Build and Run Query"
L135:   * On the left will be the formal query (see cite96†tons of examples , and cite93†the full guide to the query language )
L136:   * On the right will be a map of the results! You can zoom in on the results using the magnifying glass icon at the top left of the map.
L137: ## Quick Start (60 seconds): for Developers/Programmers
L138: 
L139: Note: this approach retrieves raw data, and while this example uses Javascript, with JSON output, the API works with effectively any language and has many output formats.
L140:   * (Be ready to ignore the following "Error: encoding error: Your input contains only whitespace." which just means "no query was given")
L141:   * Open cite134†https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter†overpass-api.de in a new tab
L142:   * Open your browser's cite135†console†appuals.com while on that page
L143:   * Paste the code snippet below (and press `↵ Enter`)
L144: 
L145:     var query = `
L146:       [bbox:30.618338,-96.323712,30.591028,-96.330826]
L147:       [out:json]
L148:       [timeout:90]
L149:       ;
L150:       way(30.626917110746, -96.348809105664, 30.634468750236, -96.339893442898);
L151:       out geom;
L152:     `;
L153:     var result = await fetch(
L154:       "https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter",
L155:       {
L156:         method: "POST",
L157:         body: "data=" + encodeURIComponent(query),
L158:       }
L159:     ).then((data) => data.json());
L160: 
L161:     console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2));
L162:   * You should then see something similar to the following:
L163: 
L164:       {
L165:         version: 0.6,
L166:         generator: "Overpass API 0.7.61.5 4133829e",
L167:         osm3s: {

L169:           copyright: "The data included in this document is from www.openstreetmap.org. The data "...
L170:         },

L172:           {
L173:             type: "way",

L176:               minlat: 30.6277358,

L179:               maxlon: -96.340566
L180:             },
L181:             nodes: [ 222454378, 4204990218, 222454386 ],
L182:             geometry: [
L183:               { lat: 30.6277358, lon: -96.340566 },
L184:               { lat: 30.6278459, lon: -96.3407026 },
L185:               { lat: 30.628834, lon: -96.341929 }
L186:             ],
L187:             tags: {
L188:               highway: "service",
L189:               name: "W-X Street",
L190:               postal_code: "77840",
L191:               "tiger:county": "Brazos, TX"
L192:             }
L193:           },
L194:

L196:   * Usually, the output will be truncated. To see the full response:
L197:

L203: ## Public Overpass API instances
L204: 
L205: cite136†Image: Warning†upload.wikimedia.org | Free public servers are designed for small projects and can often become overloaded. Consider deploying your own server cite137†[1]†dev.overpass-api.de or using a commercial provider. Or download the regional dumps cite138†[2]†download.geofabrik.de and filter it using osmium cite139†[3]†osmcode.org L206: Typically, each Overpass instance has its own cite140†Overpass Turbo web interface.
L207: However, in the Server section of the settings, you can specify the API endpoint of another instance. Important: do not add `interpreter`, Turbo does this automatically.
L208: ### Instances with global data coverage

L211: cite142†Main Overpass API instance†overpass-api.de cite143†Operated by FOSSGIS†www.fossgis.de | `https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter`  | 0.7.62.11 87bfad18  | ﻿yes  | 2 servers, each 16 physical cores, 128 GB RAM, NVME-SSD  | You can assume that you don't disturb other users when you do less than 10,000 queries per day and download less than 1 GB data per day^{cite144†[1] }. That limit is fine for a one-off use of Overpass.
L212: If you set something up that uses the Overpass API regularly, then divide those numbers by 100 (making less than 100 queries fetching less 10 MB of data per day fine). If you have an app or website, then the usage counts towards the sum of requests made by all your users^{cite145†[2] }. Be sure to check that your app or website adds `User-Agent` or `Referer` headers to requests that uniquely identify your app^{cite146†[3] }. title: runner
description: Set up and tune this repository's trail runners.
---

Manage the trail runner configs in `.entire/runners/`.

```bash
entire runner SUBCOMMAND
```

`entire runner` is experimental and appears under [labs](/cli-reference/labs). A [runner](/glossary#runner) scores and reviews a branch's changes; this command manages the per-repository set: risk, confidence, drift, security, review, and others.

## runner setup

Create and tailor this repository's trail runners.

```bash
entire runner setup [RUNNER] [flags]
```

`setup` customizes runner templates using repository documentation and structure, merged pull requests, issues, frequently changed code, and past trail findings.

Without an action flag, `setup` opens an interactive action picker. In a non-interactive environment, you must pass `--yes`, `--defaults-only`, `--print-prompt`, or `--dry-run`.

Pass a runner name, such as `risk` or `trail-risk`, to customize only that runner.

Customization uses your configured summary provider. If none is configured and several agents are installed, Entire asks which to use. Pass `--agent NAME` to select one for this run without saving the choice.

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--agent NAME` | Text-generation agent to use for customization. Only applies to `--yes`, `--dry-run`, or customization selected in the picker. |
| `--debug-dir DIRECTORY` | Write the prompt as `prompt.txt` and, when a provider runs, its raw response as `response.txt`, to this directory. |
| `--defaults-only` | Create generic default runners and stop. Does not call a provider. |
| `--dry-run` | Run customization and show the result as a diff without writing runner files, even in a repository with no runners. |
| `--limit N` | How many recent pull requests, issues, and trails to sample. Defaults to `20`. |
| `--print-prompt` | Create defaults if missing, then print the customization prompt instead of running a provider. |
| `--run` | Deprecated alias for `--yes`. |
| `--sources SOURCES` | Comma-separated data sources to gather: `repo`, `prs`, `checkpoints`, `trails`, or `all`. Defaults to `all`. |
| `-y, --yes` | Create defaults if missing, then customize runners in place. Add `--agent` to skip provider selection too. |

`--defaults-only`, `--print-prompt`, and `--dry-run` are mutually exclusive and take precedence over `--yes`.

```bash
# Print the customization prompt for every runner
entire runner setup --print-prompt

# Create defaults if missing and customize them with Codex
entire runner setup --yes --agent codex

# Preview changes to the risk runner using repository data only
entire runner setup risk --dry-run --sources repo --agent codex
```

<Warning>
`--yes` and customization selected in the picker rewrite files in `.entire/runners/`. Review changes with `git diff -- .entire/runners/` before committing.
</Warning>

  </Card>

    See how runners and trails fit together.

title: runner
description: Set up and tune this repository's trail runners.
---

Manage the trail runner configs in `.entire/runners/`.

```bash
entire runner SUBCOMMAND
```

`entire runner` is experimental and appears under [labs](/cli-reference/labs). A [runner](/glossary#runner) scores and reviews a branch's changes; this command manages the per-repository set: risk, confidence, drift, security, review, and others.

## runner setup

Create and tailor this repository's trail runners.

```bash
entire runner setup [RUNNER] [flags]
```

`setup` customizes runner templates using repository documentation and structure, merged pull requests, issues, frequently changed code, and past trail findings.

Without an action flag, `setup` opens an interactive action picker. In a non-interactive environment, you must pass `--yes`, `--defaults-only`, `--print-prompt`, or `--dry-run`.

Pass a runner name, such as `risk` or `trail-risk`, to customize only that runner.

Customization uses your configured summary provider. If none is configured and several agents are installed, Entire asks which to use. Pass `--agent NAME` to select one for this run without saving the choice.

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--agent NAME` | Text-generation agent to use for customization. Only applies to `--yes`, `--dry-run`, or customization selected in the picker. |
| `--debug-dir DIRECTORY` | Write the prompt as `prompt.txt` and, when a provider runs, its raw response as `response.txt`, to this directory. |
| `--defaults-only` | Create generic default runners and stop. Does not call a provider. |
| `--dry-run` | Run customization and show the result as a diff without writing runner files, even in a repository with no runners. |
| `--limit N` | How many recent pull requests, issues, and trails to sample. Defaults to `20`. |
| `--print-prompt` | Create defaults if missing, then print the customization prompt instead of running a provider. |
| `--run` | Deprecated alias for `--yes`. |
| `--sources SOURCES` | Comma-separated data sources to gather: `repo`, `prs`, `checkpoints`, `trails`, or `all`. Defaults to `all`. |
| `-y, --yes` | Create defaults if missing, then customize runners in place. Add `--agent` to skip provider selection too. |

`--defaults-only`, `--print-prompt`, and `--dry-run` are mutually exclusive and take precedence over `--yes`.

```bash
# Print the customization prompt for every runner
entire runner setup --print-prompt

# Create defaults if missing and customize them with Codex
entire runner setup --yes --agent codex

# Preview changes to the risk runner using repository data only
entire runner setup risk --dry-run --sources repo --agent codex
```

<Warning>
`--yes` and customization selected in the picker rewrite files in `.entire/runners/`. Review changes with `git diff -- .entire/runners/` before committing.
</Warning>

Set up the .entire/runners/*.json evaluators for this repository.

Runners (risk, confidence, drift, security, review, …) score and review a
branch's changes. The shipped defaults are generic; setup can tailor them to
THIS repo using gathered signal — its docs and structure, merged PRs and
issues, checkpoint churn hotspots, and past trail findings.

In a terminal with no flags, setup asks whether you want the generic defaults
or defaults tailored to this repo. Otherwise name the action up front:

  -y, --yes           create the defaults if missing, then tailor them in place
      --defaults-only create the generic defaults and stop
      --print-prompt  create the defaults if missing, then print the tailoring prompt for your own agent to run
      --dry-run       show the tailoring as a diff and write nothing

--yes and --dry-run each call your configured summary provider once. With no
provider configured and several agents installed, you are asked which to use;
pass --agent <name> to name one for this run instead (nothing is saved).
Review a tailoring with git diff .entire/runners.

If <runner> is given (e.g. "risk" or "trail-risk"), only that runner is tuned.

      --debug-dir string   Write the assembled prompt (prompt.txt) and, when a provider runs, its raw response (response.txt) to this directory for debugging
      --defaults-only      Create the generic default runners and stop (no tailoring, no provider call)
      --dry-run            Show the tailoring as a diff and write nothing
  -h, --help               help for setup

      --print-prompt       Create the default runners if missing, then print the tailoring prompt for your own agent instead of running a provider

Make an authenticated HTTP request to an Entire API and print the JSON response.

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to core   the control plane (default): orgs, repos, mirrors, clusters, /me
  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

Use --jurisdiction <slug> (e.g. us, eu) to reach a specific jurisdiction's
entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo
  {repo_id}        the repo's Entire ULID (from its mirror) — cells key on this

The method is GET unless a field/body is given (then POST); override with -X.

  entire api --to cell /api/v1/me/activity
  entire api --jurisdiction eu /api/v1/me/activity

  entire api -X POST /api/v1/projects -f name=demo

These endpoints are internal and can change shape without notice; where a
purpose-built command exists, its output is the stable interface.

The CLI attaches the right bearer token and dials the right host for the
chosen backend, so you don't have to plumb auth yourself:

  --to cell   your home entire-api cell: /me/* activity, repo aggregates

entire-api cell instead of your home one; it implies --to cell.

<path> is the full path on that host, e.g. /api/v1/clusters. These
placeholders are filled from the current repo's origin remote:
  {owner} {repo}   the GitHub owner / repo

  async (c) => {
    const pre = await resolveNumberedRepoContext(c)
    if (pre instanceof Response) return pre
    const { trailNumber } = pre
    const cell = await pre.resolveCell()
    if (cell instanceof Response) return cell
    if (cell) {
      const row = cell.trail
      // Native branches are updated by entire-api, never through a same-slug GitHub mirror.
      if (cell.provider === "et") {
        const upstream = await proxyEntireApiWrite(
          c,
          entireApiTrailWriteOptions(c, {
            method: "POST",
            pathFor: (repoId) => `repos/${repoId}/trails/${trailNumber}/update-branch`,
            projectResponse: true,
            // A native merge may outlive the ordinary proxy deadline. Let the
            // cell own the irreversible operation just like final Trail merge.
            upstreamFetchTimeoutMs: TRAIL_MERGE_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS,
          }),
        )
        return projectEntireApiWriteResponse(upstream, {
          normalize: (payload) => {
            const p = payload as { mergeCommitSha?: string }
            return { ok: true, merge_commit_sha: p.mergeCommitSha ?? "" }
          },
        })
      }
      if (!row.branch) return c.json({ error: "Trail has no linked branch" }, 422)
      const token = await resolveUserGitHubTokenOrResponse(c)
      if (token instanceof Response) return token
      try {
        // Cell detail intentionally has no shadow-PR id. Resolve the open PR by
        // its same-repo head branch so a retargeted PR's live base wins over the
        // cell's last stored base, matching the legacy active-base behavior.
        //
        // This is a deliberate split from the sessions/files read paths, which
        // trust the cell's stored base and skip this lookup entirely: that base
        // has been authoritative since ENT-1688's retargetTrailBase, so a live
        // check there would just be a redundant round-trip. This route is a
        // write (merge), so it pays that round-trip for freshness before
        // mutating. /checks above keeps its own live base too, but for free —
        // it already fetches the PR for activePr?.number, so no extra call.
        const activePr = await findOpenPullRequestForHead(cell.repoFullName, row.branch, token)
        const base = activePr?.base ?? resolveBaseBranch(row, cell.repo)
        const comparison = await compareBranchStatus(cell.repoFullName, base, row.branch, token)
        if (!comparison) {
          return c.json(
            {
              error: "Could not verify whether this branch is up to date",
              comparison_status: "unknown",
            },
            422,
          )
        }
        if (comparison.behind_by === 0) {
          await triggerTrailGateRecompute(c, pre.trailNumber, cell.repoFullName)
          return c.json({ ok: true, merge_commit_sha: "" })
        }
        const result = await mergeBranch(
          cell.repoFullName,
          base,
          row.branch,
          `Merge branch '${base}' into ${row.branch}`,
          token,
        )
        await c.env.ENTIRE_CACHE.delete(`trail-checks:${cell.repoFullName}:${row.number}`)
        return c.json({ ok: true, merge_commit_sha: result.sha })
      } catch (err) {
        if (isGitHubAuthError(err)) return c.json({ error: "GitHub token expired" }, 401)
        if (err instanceof Error && err.message.startsWith("Merge conflict")) {
          return c.json(
            { error: "Branch has conflicts with the base branch that must be resolved manually" },
            409,
          )
        }
        recordSpanError(err)
        return c.json({ error: "Failed to update branch" }, 500)
      }
    }

    return cellRoutedRefusal(c)
  },
)

async function getTrailFilesHandler(c: TrailContext, ctx: TrailEntireApiContext) {
  const { trail: row } = ctx
  const historyBranch = row.branch ?? row.original_branch
  const snapshotBase = row.merge_base_sha ?? row.base_sha
  const snapshotHead = row.head_sha
  const hasSnapshotRefs =
    (row.status === "merged" || row.status === "closed") && snapshotBase && snapshotHead

  if (!historyBranch && !hasSnapshotRefs) {
    c.header("x-trail-files-source", "none")
    return c.json({
      files: [],
      additions: 0,
      deletions: 0,
      truncated: false,
      head_sha: null,
    })
  }
  if (!getEntireApiTrailReadParams(c, ctx)) {
    c.header("x-trail-files-source", "none")
    return c.json({ error: "Changed files require a browser session" }, 501)
  }

  let entireApiResult
  try {
    entireApiResult = await fetchEntireApiTrailFiles(c, ctx)
  } catch (err) {
    console.warn(`Failed to fetch entire-api trail files ${row.number}:`, err)
    recordSpanError(err)
    return c.json({ error: "Changed files unavailable" }, 503)
  }
  if (!entireApiResult) {
    c.header("x-trail-files-source", "none")
    return c.json({ error: "Changed files unavailable" }, 503)
  }
  c.header("x-trail-files-source", "entire-api")
  return c.json(entireApiResult)
}

// POST /:host/:owner/:repo/:number/runs/:runnerId — Trigger a cell-native Trail runner.
// This is a Trail command, not the retired BFF sandbox-run lifecycle: entire-api
// owns runner selection, execution, deduplication, and persistence.
trailRoutes.post(
  "/:host/:owner/:repo/:number/runs/:runnerId",
  describeRoute({
    tags: ["Trails"],
    summary: "Trigger a configured trail runner",
    responses: {
      200: {
        description: "Trail runner started or reused",
        content: { "application/json": { schema: resolver(trailRunTriggerSchema) } },
      },
      422: {
        description: "Trail runner unavailable",
        content: { "application/json": { schema: resolver(errorSchema) } },
      },
    },
  }),
  async (c) => {
    const pre = await resolveNumberedRepoContext(c)
    if (pre instanceof Response) return pre
    const runnerId = c.req.param("runnerId") ?? ""
    if (!isValidRunnerId(runnerId)) return c.json({ error: "Invalid runner id" }, 400)

    const body = (await c.req.text()) || undefined
    return proxyEntireApiWrite(
      c,
      entireApiTrailWriteOptions(c, {
        method: "POST",
        pathFor: (repoId) => `repos/${repoId}/trails/${pre.trailNumber}/runs/${runnerId}`,
        body,
      }),
    )
  },
)

// POST /:host/:owner/:repo/:number/review-rerun — Ask entire-api to rerun the
// configured push review for the trail's current head.
trailRoutes.post(
  "/:host/:owner/:repo/:number/review-rerun",
  describeRoute({
    tags: ["Trails"],
    summary: "Re-run the configured review for the current head",
    responses: {
      200: {
        description: "Review re-run started or already running",
        content: {
          "application/json": { schema: resolver(z.object({ launched: z.number() })) },
        },
      },
      422: {
        description: "No push-triggered review runner is configured",
        content: { "application/json": { schema: resolver(errorSchema) } },
      },
    },
  }),
  async (c) => {
    const pre = await resolveNumberedRepoContext(c)
    if (pre instanceof Response) return pre
    const membershipError = requireRepoMembership(c, pre.base)
    if (membershipError) return membershipError
    const body = (await c.req.text()) || undefined
    return proxyEntireApiWrite(
      c,
      entireApiTrailWriteOptions(c, {
        method: "POST",
        pathFor: (repoId) => `repos/${repoId}/trails/${pre.trailNumber}/review-rerun`,
        body,
      }),
    )
  },
)

  async (c) => {
    const pre = await resolveNumberedRepoContext(c)
    if (pre instanceof Response) return pre
    const { trailNumber } = pre
    const cell = await pre.resolveCell()
    if (cell instanceof Response) return cell
    if (cell) {
      const row = cell.trail
      // Native branches are updated by entire-api, never through a same-slug GitHub mirror.
      if (cell.provider === "et") {
        const upstream = await proxyEntireApiWrite(
          c,
          entireApiTrailWriteOptions(c, {
            method: "POST",
            pathFor: (repoId) => `repos/${repoId}/trails/${trailNumber}/update-branch`,
            projectResponse: true,
            // A native merge may outlive the ordinary proxy deadline. Let the
            // cell own the irreversible operation just like final Trail merge.
            upstreamFetchTimeoutMs: TRAIL_MERGE_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS,
          }),
        )
        return projectEntireApiWriteResponse(upstream, {
          normalize: (payload) => {
            const p = payload as { mergeCommitSha?: string }
            return { ok: true, merge_commit_sha: p.mergeCommitSha ?? "" }
          },
        })
      }
      if (!row.branch) return c.json({ error: "Trail has no linked branch" }, 422)
      const token = await resolveUserGitHubTokenOrResponse(c)
      if (token instanceof Response) return token
      try {
        // Cell detail intentionally has no shadow-PR id. Resolve the open PR by
        // its same-repo head branch so a retargeted PR's live base wins over the
        // cell's last stored base, matching the legacy active-base behavior.
        //
        // This is a deliberate split from the sessions/files read paths, which
        // trust the cell's stored base and skip this lookup entirely: that base
        // has been authoritative since ENT-1688's retargetTrailBase, so a live
        // check there would just be a redundant round-trip. This route is a
        // write (merge), so it pays that round-trip for freshness before
        // mutating. /checks above keeps its own live base too, but for free —
        // it already fetches the PR for activePr?.number, so no extra call.
        const activePr = await findOpenPullRequestForHead(cell.repoFullName, row.branch, token)
        const base = activePr?.base ?? resolveBaseBranch(row, cell.repo)
        const comparison = await compareBranchStatus(cell.repoFullName, base, row.branch, token)
        if (!comparison) {
          return c.json(
            {
              error: "Could not verify whether this branch is up to date",
              comparison_status: "unknown",
            },
            422,
          )
        }
        if (comparison.behind_by === 0) {
          await triggerTrailGateRecompute(c, pre.trailNumber, cell.repoFullName)
          return c.json({ ok: true, merge_commit_sha: "" })
        }
        const result = await mergeBranch(
          cell.repoFullName,
          base,
          row.branch,
          `Merge branch '${base}' into ${row.branch}`,
          token,
        )
        await c.env.ENTIRE_CACHE.delete(`trail-checks:${cell.repoFullName}:${row.number}`)
        return c.json({ ok: true, merge_commit_sha: result.sha })
      } catch (err) {
        if (isGitHubAuthError(err)) return c.json({ error: "GitHub token expired" }, 401)
        if (err instanceof Error && err.message.startsWith("Merge conflict")) {
          return c.json(
            { error: "Branch has conflicts with the base branch that must be resolved manually" },
            409,
          )
        }
        recordSpanError(err)
        return c.json({ error: "Failed to update branch" }, 500)
      }
    }

    return cellRoutedRefusal(c)
  },
)

async function getTrailFilesHandler(c: TrailContext, ctx: TrailEntireApiContext) {
  const { trail: row } = ctx
  const historyBranch = row.branch ?? row.original_branch
  const snapshotBase = row.merge_base_sha ?? row.base_sha
  const snapshotHead = row.head_sha
  const hasSnapshotRefs =
    (row.status === "merged" || row.status === "closed") && snapshotBase && snapshotHead

  if (!historyBranch && !hasSnapshotRefs) {
    c.header("x-trail-files-source", "none")
    return c.json({
      files: [],
      additions: 0,
      deletions: 0,
      truncated: false,
      head_sha: null,
    })
  }
  if (!getEntireApiTrailReadParams(c, ctx)) {
    c.header("x-trail-files-source", "none")
    return c.json({ error: "Changed files require a browser session" }, 501)
  }

  let entireApiResult
  try {
    entireApiResult = await fetchEntireApiTrailFiles(c, ctx)
  } catch (err) {
    console.warn(`Failed to fetch entire-api trail files ${row.number}:`, err)
    recordSpanError(err)
    return c.json({ error: "Changed files unavailable" }, 503)
  }
  if (!entireApiResult) {
    c.header("x-trail-files-source", "none")
    return c.json({ error: "Changed files unavailable" }, 503)
  }
  c.header("x-trail-files-source", "entire-api")
  return c.json(entireApiResult)
}

// POST /:host/:owner/:repo/:number/runs/:runnerId — Trigger a cell-native Trail runner.
// This is a Trail command, not the retired BFF sandbox-run lifecycle: entire-api
// owns runner selection, execution, deduplication, and persistence.
trailRoutes.post(
  "/:host/:owner/:repo/:number/runs/:runnerId",
  describeRoute({
    tags: ["Trails"],
    summary: "Trigger a configured trail runner",
    responses: {
      200: {
        description: "Trail runner started or reused",
        content: { "application/json": { schema: resolver(trailRunTriggerSchema) } },
      },
      422: {
        description: "Trail runner unavailable",
        content: { "application/json": { schema: resolver(errorSchema) } },
      },
    },
  }),
  async (c) => {
    const pre = await resolveNumberedRepoContext(c)
    if (pre instanceof Response) return pre

            upstreamFetchTimeoutMs: TRAIL_MERGE_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS,

        )
        return projectEntireApiWriteResponse(upstream, {
          normalize: (payload) => {
            const p = payload as { mergeCommitSha?: string }
            return { ok: true, merge_commit_sha: p.mergeCommitSha ?? "" }
          },
        })
      }
      if (!row.branch) return c.json({ error: "Trail has no linked branch" }, 422)
      const token = await resolveUserGitHubTokenOrResponse(c)
      if (token instanceof Response) return token
      try {
        // Cell detail intentionally has no shadow-PR id. Resolve the open PR by
        // its same-repo head branch so a retargeted PR's live base wins over the
        // cell's last stored base, matching the legacy active-base behavior.
        //
        // This is a deliberate split from the sessions/files read paths, which
        // trust the cell's stored base and skip this lookup entirely: that base
        // has been authoritative since ENT-1688's retargetTrailBase, so a live
        // check there would just be a redundant round-trip. This route is a
        // write (merge), so it pays that round-trip for freshness before
        // mutating. /checks above keeps its own live base too, but for free —
        // it already fetches the PR for activePr?.number, so no extra call.
        const activePr = await findOpenPullRequestForHead(cell.repoFullName, row.branch, token)
        const base = activePr?.base ?? resolveBaseBranch(row, cell.repo)
        const comparison = await compareBranchStatus(cell.repoFullName, base, row.branch, token)

          return c.json(
            {

              comparison_status: "unknown",

async function getTrailFilesHandler(c: TrailContext, ctx: TrailEntireApiContext) {
  const { trail: row } = ctx
  const historyBranch = row.branch ?? row.original_branch
  const snapshotBase = row.merge_base_sha ?? row.base_sha
  const snapshotHead = row.head_sha
  const hasSnapshotRefs =
    (row.status === "merged" || row.status === "closed") && snapshotBase && snapshotHead

  if (!historyBranch && !hasSnapshotRefs) {
    c.header("x-trail-files-source", "none")
    return c.json({
      files: [],
      additions: 0,
      deletions: 0,
      truncated: false,
      head_sha: null,
    })
  }
  if (!getEntireApiTrailReadParams(c, ctx)) {
    c.header("x-trail-files-source", "none")
    return c.json({ error: "Changed files require a browser session" }, 501)
  }

  let entireApiResult
  try {
    entireApiResult = await fetchEntireApiTrailFiles(c, ctx)
  } catch (err) {
    console.warn(`Failed to fetch entire-api trail files ${row.number}:`, err)
    recordSpanError(err)
    return c.json({ error: "Changed files unavailable" }, 503)
  }
  if (!entireApiResult) {
    c.header("x-trail-files-source", "none")
    return c.json({ error: "Changed files unavailable" }, 503)
  }
  c.header("x-trail-files-source", "entire-api")
  return c.json(entireApiResult)
}

## Goal

Refresh `sf-stairs-map/` so it feels like a locally made San Francisco stairway guide rather than a generic AI-generated landing page.

Current site: https://sf-stairs-map.lizzie-siegle5086.workers.dev

## Scope

- Replace slogan-heavy copy and stock landing-page styling with a practical, distinctive map-first design.
- Improve typography, spacing, visual hierarchy, map/list balance, and mobile use. Keep real staircase photography prominent.
- Preserve search, neighborhood and rating filters, stairway details, photo albums, map legend, and walking-direction links.
- Preserve the homage to Alexandra Kenin / Urban Hiker SF; info@urbanhikersf.com; Instagram/Twitter @urbanhikersf; Facebook facebook.com/urbanhikersf; and the book credit to Mary Burk and Adah Bakalinsky.
- Keep the sticky footer text: `made w/ <3 in sf`.
- Coordinate with the separate route-generator trail so the final layout accommodates route controls without duplicating that feature's logic.

## Acceptance

- Deliberate desktop and mobile layouts, with readable controls and no horizontal overflow.
- Keyboard-visible focus, usable dialogs, and accessible input labels.
- `npm ci`, `npm run build`, and `npm test` pass from `sf-stairs-map/`; inspect desktop and mobile screenshots.
- Entire runner findings are reviewed before merging. Deploy the verified result to the existing Cloudflare Worker after integration.

## Branch and baseline

Use `sf-stairs/design-refresh`, based on `sf-stairs/baseline`. The shared baseline contains the currently deployed site, committed as fc8b37f. Limit implementation changes to `sf-stairs-map/`. Do not merge or modify unrelated monorepo projects.
EOF
cat > /tmp/sf-stairs-trail-briefs/routes.md <<'EOF'
## Goal

Add a route generator to `sf-stairs-map/` that lets someone visit several different San Francisco staircases in one walk or run.

Current site: https://sf-stairs-map.lizzie-siegle5086.workers.dev

## Scope

- Let the user choose a starting stairway, neighborhood, and number of staircase stops, with a return-to-start option.
- Generate an ordered route, draw it on the map, and show numbered stops and distance computed from the actual path.
- Support generating an alternative route and exporting GPX or sharing the itinerary.
- Follow pedestrian-accessible streets and paths. Never present straight-line connections as runnable routes.
- Exclude unverified locations and entries without coordinates. Handle disconnected paths, insufficient nearby stairways, duplicate stops, and data-loading failures.
- Be explicit when paths reach nearby access points rather than traversing every staircase. Do not invent elevation, climb counts, precise running times, or live access guarantees.
- Keep the original map, photos, legend, source credits, and sticky `made w/ <3 in sf` footer.

## Acceptance

- Test distinct stops, loop closure, valid pedestrian graph edges, distance calculation, missing coordinates, unreachable points, alternative routes, and export/share behavior.
- `npm ci`, `npm run build`, and `npm test` pass from `sf-stairs-map/`; inspect the itinerary and map on desktop and mobile.
- Review routing-data licensing, source attribution, payload size, and access restrictions.
- Entire runner findings are reviewed before merging. Deploy the verified result to the existing Cloudflare Worker after integration.

## Branch and baseline

Use `sf-stairs/route-generator`, based on `sf-stairs/baseline`. The shared baseline contains the currently deployed site, committed as fc8b37f. Coordinate UI integration with the separate design-refresh trail. Limit implementation changes to `sf-stairs-map/`.

## Local research, not completed implementation

Before the Entire workflow was clarified, unreviewed local drafts were created in `/Users/lizziesiegle/Desktop/demos3idkman/sf-stairs-map/`: `src/routing.ts`, `scripts/import-network.py`, and `public/walking-network.json`. They are not part of the shared baseline and are not deployed. Treat them as optional research, not validated functionality.

The draft explores a bundled OpenStreetMap walking graph and A* routing, with nearby staircase access points and GPX export. Its 10 MB network needs size/performance review. The downloaded source used skeletal nodes, so node-level access/barrier tags were not retained; refresh with full node tags before relying on it. Stairway snapping does not prove a complete staircase traversal. No route UI or routing tests have been implemented.
EOF","max_output_tokens":1000}));

  "title": "Generate walking and running routes through multiple staircases",
  "body": "Goal\nAdd a route generator to sf-stairs-map/ that lets someone visit several different San Francisco staircases in one walk or run.\nCurrent site: https://sf-stairs-map.lizzie-siegle5086.workers.dev\nScope\nLet the user choose a starting stairway, neighborhood, and number of staircase stops, with a return-to-start option.\nGenerate an ordered route, draw it on the map, and show numbered stops and distance computed from the actual path.\nSupport generating an alternative route and exporting GPX or sharing the itinerary.\nFollow pedestrian-accessible streets and paths. Never present straight-line connections as runnable routes.\nExclude unverified locations and entries without coordinates. Handle disconnected paths, insufficient nearby stairways, duplicate stops, and data-loading failures.\nBe explicit when paths reach nearby access points rather than traversing every staircase. Do not invent elevation, climb counts, precise running times, or live access guarantees.\nKeep the original map, photos, legend, source credits, and sticky made w/ \u003c3 in sf footer.\nAcceptance\nTest distinct stops, loop closure, valid pedestrian graph edges, distance calculation, missing coordinates, unreachable points, alternative routes, and export/share behavior.\nnpm ci, npm run build, and npm test pass from sf-stairs-map/; inspect the itinerary and map on desktop and mobile.\nReview routing-data licensing, source attribution, payload size, and access restrictions.\nEntire runner findings are reviewed before merging. Deploy the verified result to the existing Cloudflare Worker after integration.\nBranch and baseline\nUse sf-stairs/route-generator, based on sf-stairs/baseline. The shared baseline contains the currently deployed site, committed as fc8b37f. Coordinate UI integration with the separate design-refresh trail. Limit implementation changes to sf-stairs-map/.\nLocal research, not completed implementation\nBefore the Entire workflow was clarified, unreviewed local drafts were created in /Users/lizziesiegle/Desktop/demos3idkman/sf-stairs-map/: src/routing.ts, scripts/import-network.py, and public/walking-network.json. They are not part of the shared baseline and are not deployed. Treat them as optional research, not validated functionality.\nThe draft explores a bundled OpenStreetMap walking graph and A* routing, with nearby staircase access points and GPX export. Its 10 MB network needs size/performance review. The downloaded source used skeletal nodes, so node-level access/barrier tags were not retained; refresh with full node tags before relying on it. Stairway snapping does not prove a complete staircase traversal. No route UI or routing tests have been implemented.",

content.text:
make an interactive map website hosted on cloudflare workers based on this
  map of san francisco stairs.
  https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1OHwJvr7IrhPZ4nCelzOnPeDp3Rl567uNnyt
  P0bF8gtE/edit?gid=0#gid=0

  Based on the index of Stairway Walks of San Francisco by Mary Burk and Adah
  Bakalinsky

  reference and pay homage to: Contact: info@urbanhikersf.com
  Instagram/Twitter: @urbanhikersf
  Facebook: www.facebook.com/urbanhikersf

  include photos and the legend.

  then deploy to cloudflare workers. include a "made w/ <3 in sf" sticky footer.
this is a good start. make a trail and enable runners to make it look less ai-generated. make another trail and enable runners to add a route generator to hit up different staircases in one route

> By “make a trail and enable runners,” do you mean two parallel workstreams, or running features in the website? I’m proceeding with the design refresh and staircase route generator.

make an entire trail and enable entire runners

  Bakalinsky

  reference and pay homage to: Contact: info@urbanhikersf.com
  Instagram/Twitter: @urbanhikersf
  Facebook: www.facebook.com/urbanhikersf

  include photos and the legend.

  then deploy to cloudflare workers. include a "made w/ <3 in sf" sticky footer.

make an entire trail and enable entire runners

You are an expert, pragmatic software engineer. Deliver clean, maintainable,
production-ready code that solves the problem with minimal complexity.

- **Pragmatic and concise:** Write straightforward code. Avoid over-engineering,

- **Self-reliant:** Search the local workspace thoroughly before asking questions.
  Read definitions and existing patterns first.

## Code Quality and Standards

- **Idiomatic code:** Follow the style guides, linting rules, and formatting
  conventions native to the language in use.
- **Type safety:** Prefer strict typing, explicit interfaces, and clear schemas over
  dynamic or loose structures.
- **Zero warnings:** Code must build cleanly, with no compiler warnings, deprecation
  notices, or linter errors.
- **Error handling:** Fail fast, handle edge cases, and write meaningful log messages.

## Workflow and Execution

- **Incremental changes:** Propose and execute modifications in small, logically
  isolated, testable steps.
- **Preserve context:** Do not delete existing comments, documentation, or apparently
  unused utility code unless asked.
- **Verification:** Run the project's tests or build commands to verify changes before
  calling a task complete. If nothing covers the code you touched, say so.

## Absolute Constraints

- **No placeholders:** Never emit `// TODO`, `...`, or truncated code blocks. Provide
  full, operational implementations.
- **No hallucinated packages:** Do not add third-party dependencies unless they are
  verified as necessary and standard for the ecosystem.

---

## Communication and Writing Standard

### Objective

Optimize for reader attention.

Be concise without omitting information that changes a decision, reveals a risk,
explains a failure, or tells the user what they need to do next.

Do not optimize for appearing thorough. Optimize for useful information per word.

### Response Style

Default to short answers.

For normal coding tasks, the final response should usually be:

- 3-6 bullets, or
- fewer than ~120 words.

Only exceed this when:

- the user explicitly asks for a detailed explanation;
- there are multiple material risks or failures;
- the change involves security, data loss, migrations, compatibility, or irreversible
  actions;
- debugging requires explaining a non-obvious causal chain.

#### Final responses

Report:

1. What changed.
2. Anything important or surprising.
3. Validation performed.
4. Blockers or unresolved risks, if any.

Omit any item that has nothing useful to say.

Do not:

- restate the user's request;
- narrate your work step-by-step;
- give a development diary;
- repeat the same conclusion in a summary;
- add introductory filler;
- explain obvious code;
- describe every file touched unless the files themselves matter;
- end with generic statements such as "Let me know if you need anything else."

Prefer bullets to paragraphs when communicating multiple facts.

Put the most important information first.

If one sentence is sufficient, use one sentence.

### Code Comments

The default is NO comment.

Code should explain WHAT it does through names, types, structure, and decomposition.
Comments should explain WHY when the reason cannot be made obvious in code.

Add a comment only when it communicates something such as:

- a non-obvious invariant;
- an external constraint;
- a compatibility requirement;
- a deliberate workaround;
- a security or performance tradeoff;
- behavior that appears incorrect but is intentional;
- information needed to prevent a future maintainer from making a plausible mistake.

Before adding a comment, ask:

> Could clearer naming, typing, or structure make this comment unnecessary?

If yes, improve the code instead.

Do not add comments that:

- restate the following line of code;
- translate syntax into English;
- announce a function or loop;
- describe information already obvious from names or types;
- preserve implementation history that belongs in git;
- add headings to self-explanatory blocks;
- use lengthy prose for straightforward behavior.

Keep ordinary comments to 1-2 lines.

Long comments are reserved for genuinely complex invariants, protocols, algorithms,
external constraints, or dangerous edge cases.

Apply the same standard to docstrings. Do not document obvious parameters or return
values merely because a docstring format permits it.

### Technical Writing Standard

Use simplified technical English. This is STE100-inspired guidance, not a requirement
for strict STE100 compliance.

Prefer:

- short declarative sentences;
- active voice;
- one main idea per sentence;
- common words over formal words;
- concrete nouns and verbs;
- consistent terminology;
- explicit subjects;
- established domain terminology.

Avoid:

- invented jargon;
- unnecessary acronyms;
- multiple names for the same concept;
- vague references such as "this", "that", or "it" when the referent is unclear;
- long noun chains;
- filler words;
- unnecessary adjectives and adverbs;
- inflated phrases when a short word says the same thing.

If a technical term is necessary, use it consistently. Do not invent a synonym to
make the prose sound less repetitive.

Follow Zinsser's four principles: clarity, simplicity, brevity, humanity.

Clarity outranks brevity. Never remove information required to understand the
decision, risk, or behavior.

### Cold Reader Test

For PR descriptions, review comments, code comments, docstrings, commit messages, and
important explanatory text, assume the reader has NO context from the current agent
conversation.

Before finishing, ask:

- Can a competent engineer understand what this means without the chat history?
- Is the reason for the change clear?
- Are important assumptions explicit?
- Is any term invented or unnecessarily specialized?
- Does every pronoun have an obvious referent?
- Is any sentence saying something the reader already knows?
- Can anything be deleted without losing useful meaning?

Delete text that fails the final test.

Do not compensate for unclear writing by adding more writing. Rewrite it.

### Pull Request Writing

PRs are reference material, not development diaries.

A PR body should make these things easy to discover:

- Why the change exists.
- What materially changed.
- How it was validated.
- Important risks, tradeoffs, or follow-up work.

Use short sections and bullets.

Do not list routine implementation details visible in the diff.

Do not describe abandoned approaches unless understanding them prevents a likely
future mistake.

Review the PR title, PR body, code comments, and explanatory prose separately from
code correctness.

### Review Comments

Lead with the finding.

Preferred:

> `parseConfig()` accepts an empty token here, so malformed configs reach the
> executor. Reject the empty value before constructing `Config`.

Avoid:

> I was looking through this section and noticed that there might potentially be
> an issue with how we're handling configuration values here...

Review comments should normally contain:

- the problem;
- why it matters;
- the required change, when non-obvious.

Do not include praise, narration, or background unless it changes the reader's
understanding.

One finding per comment.

---

## Agent-Specific Behavior

### Implementation agents

Prioritize implementation over explanation.

Do not add explanatory comments merely because the code was AI-generated.

Final response: result, validation, material caveats.

### Exploration and research agents

Do the verbose exploration internally. Return only information needed by the calling
agent.

Default to no more than 5 findings.

Do not return search logs, dead ends, or a narrative of how you investigated.

### Code review agents

Return actionable findings first. For each finding include:

- severity when useful;
- location;
- failure mode or risk;
- recommended fix when non-obvious.

Do not summarize unchanged code. Do not invent findings to make the review look
comprehensive. If there are no material findings, say so briefly.

### Writing-review agents

Review writing independently of code correctness.

Focus on:

- PR title and body;
- code comments and docstrings;
- user-facing strings;
- commit messages when requested;
- prose introduced in the diff.

Evaluate:

1. Cold-reader comprehension.
2. Unnecessary words.
3. Invented or inconsistent terminology.
4. Ambiguity.
5. STE100-inspired simplicity.
6. Zinsser: clarity, simplicity, brevity, humanity.

Prefer deletion over rewriting when text adds no useful information. Return only
actionable findings.

---

## Priority Rule

Conciseness must never hide:

- failures;
- uncertainty;
- material risks;
- breaking changes;
- security implications;
- data-loss risk;
- incomplete validation;
- assumptions that materially affect correctness.

Everything else must earn its words.

Prefer deletion over rewriting when text adds no useful information. Return only
actionable findings.

---

## Priority Rule

Conciseness must never hide:

- failures;
- uncertainty;
- material risks;
- breaking changes;
- security implications;
- data-loss risk;
- incomplete validation;
- assumptions that materially affect correctness.

Everything else must earn its words.

Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. (file: r2/imagegen/SKILL.md)

Covers Agent class, state management, callable RPC, Workflows, durable execution, queues, retries, observability, and React hooks. Biases towards retrieval from Cloudflare docs over pre-trained knowledge. (file: r0/agents-sdk/SKILL.md)

# Cloudflare Platform Skill

Consolidated skill for building on the Cloudflare platform. Use decision trees below to find the right product, then load detailed references.

Your knowledge of Cloudflare APIs, types, limits, and pricing may be outdated. **Prefer retrieval over pre-training** — the references in this skill are starting points, not source of truth.

## Retrieval Sources

Fetch the **latest** information before citing specific numbers, API signatures, or configuration options. Do not rely on baked-in knowledge or these reference files alone.

| Source | How to retrieve | Use for |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| Cloudflare docs | Cloudflare MCP `docs` tool or `https://developers.cloudflare.com/` | Limits, pricing, API reference, compatibility dates/flags |
| Workers types | `npm pack @cloudflare/workers-types` or check `node_modules` | Type signatures, binding shapes, handler types |
| Wrangler config schema | `node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json` | Config fields, binding shapes, allowed values |
| Product changelogs | `https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/` | Recent changes to limits, features, deprecations |

When a reference file and the docs disagree, **trust the docs**. This is especially important for: numeric limits, pricing tiers, type signatures, and configuration options.

## Quick Decision Trees

### "I need feature flags"

```
Need feature flags?
└─ Feature toggles, targeting rules, percentage rollouts → flagship/
   ├─ Evaluate in Workers → Flagship binding (env.FLAGS)
   ├─ Evaluate in Node.js / browser → OpenFeature SDK (@cloudflare/flagship)
   └─ Manage flags via API → Flagship REST API
```

### "I need to run code"

```
Need to run code?
├─ Serverless functions at the edge → workers/
├─ Full-stack web app with Git deploys → pages/
├─ Stateful coordination/real-time → durable-objects/
├─ Long-running multi-step jobs → workflows/
├─ Run containers → containers/
├─ Multi-tenant (customers deploy code) → workers-for-platforms/
├─ Scheduled tasks (cron) → cron-triggers/
├─ Lightweight edge logic (modify HTTP) → snippets/
├─ Process Worker execution events (logs/observability) → tail-workers/
└─ Optimize latency to backend infrastructure → smart-placement/
```

### "I need to store data"

```
Need storage?
├─ Key-value (config, sessions, cache) → kv/
├─ Relational SQL → d1/ (SQLite) or hyperdrive/ (existing Postgres/MySQL)
├─ Object/file storage (S3-compatible) → r2/
```

# Cloudflare Platform Skill

Consolidated skill for building on the Cloudflare platform. Use decision trees below to find the right product, then load detailed references.

Your knowledge of Cloudflare APIs, types, limits, and pricing may be outdated. **Prefer retrieval over pre-training** — the references in this skill are starting points, not source of truth.

## Retrieval Sources

Fetch the **latest** information before citing specific numbers, API signatures, or configuration options. Do not rely on baked-in knowledge or these reference files alone.

| Source | How to retrieve | Use for |
|--------|----------------|---------|
| Cloudflare docs | Cloudflare MCP `docs` tool or `https://developers.cloudflare.com/` | Limits, pricing, API reference, compatibility dates/flags |
| Workers types | `npm pack @cloudflare/workers-types` or check `node_modules` | Type signatures, binding shapes, handler types |
| Wrangler config schema | `node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json` | Config fields, binding shapes, allowed values |
| Product changelogs | `https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/` | Recent changes to limits, features, deprecations |

When a reference file and the docs disagree, **trust the docs**. This is especially important for: numeric limits, pricing tiers, type signatures, and configuration options.

## Quick Decision Trees

### "I need feature flags"

```
Need feature flags?
└─ Feature toggles, targeting rules, percentage rollouts → flagship/
   ├─ Evaluate in Workers → Flagship binding (env.FLAGS)
   ├─ Evaluate in Node.js / browser → OpenFeature SDK (@cloudflare/flagship)
   └─ Manage flags via API → Flagship REST API
```

### "I need to run code"

```
Need to run code?
├─ Serverless functions at the edge → workers/
├─ Full-stack web app with Git deploys → pages/
├─ Stateful coordination/real-time → durable-objects/
├─ Long-running multi-step jobs → workflows/
├─ Run containers → containers/
├─ Multi-tenant (customers deploy code) → workers-for-platforms/
├─ Scheduled tasks (cron) → cron-triggers/
├─ Lightweight edge logic (modify HTTP) → snippets/
├─ Process Worker execution events (logs/observability) → tail-workers/
└─ Optimize latency to backend infrastructure → smart-placement/
```

### "I need to store data"

```
Need storage?
├─ Key-value (config, sessions, cache) → kv/
├─ Relational SQL → d1/ (SQLite) or hyperdrive/ (existing Postgres/MySQL)
├─ Object/file storage (S3-compatible) → r2/
├─ Versioned file trees (repos, build outputs, checkpoints) → artifacts/
├─ Message queue (async processing) → queues/
├─ Vector embeddings (AI/semantic search) → vectorize/
├─ Strongly-consistent per-entity state → durable-objects/ (DO storage)
├─ Secrets management → secrets-store/
├─ Streaming ETL to R2 → pipelines/
├─ Managed Apache Iceberg catalog on R2 → r2-data-catalog/
├─ Serverless SQL analytics over Iceberg tables → r2-sql/
└─ Persistent cache (long-term retention) → cache-reserve/
```

### "I need AI/ML"

```
Need AI?
├─ Run inference (LLMs, embeddings, images) → workers-ai/
├─ Vector database for RAG/search → vectorize/
├─ Build stateful AI agents → agents-sdk/
├─ Gateway for any AI provider (caching, routing) → ai-gateway/
└─ AI-powered search widget → ai-search/
```

### "I need networking/connectivity"

```
Need networking?
├─ Expose local service to internet → tunnel/
├─ TCP/UDP proxy (non-HTTP) → spectrum/
├─ WebRTC TURN server → turn/
├─ Private network connectivity → network-interconnect/
├─ Optimize routing → argo-smart-routing/
├─ Optimize latency to backend (not user) → smart-placement/
└─ Real-time video/audio → realtimekit/ or realtime-sfu/
```

### "I need security"

```
Need security?
├─ Web Application Firewall → waf/
├─ DDoS protection → ddos/
├─ Bot detection/management → bot-management/
├─ API protection → api-shield/
├─ CAPTCHA alternative → turnstile/
└─ Credential leak detection → waf/ (managed ruleset)
```

### "I need media/content"

```
Need media?
├─ Image optimization/transformation → images/
├─ Video streaming/encoding → stream/
├─ Browser automation/screenshots → browser-rendering/
└─ Third-party script management → zaraz/
```

### "I need analytics/metrics data"

```
Need analytics?
├─ Query across all Cloudflare products (HTTP, Workers, DNS, etc.) → graphql-api/
├─ Custom high-cardinality metrics from Workers → analytics-engine/
├─ Client-side (RUM) performance data → web-analytics/
├─ Workers Logs and real-time debugging → observability/
├─ SQL over Iceberg data lake (logs, events) → r2-sql/ (+ pipelines/, r2-data-catalog/)
└─ Raw logs (Logpush to external tools) → Cloudflare docs
```

### "I need infrastructure-as-code"

```
Need IaC? → pulumi/ (Pulumi), terraform/ (Terraform), or api/ (REST API)
```

# Geocode an address Stay organized with collections Save and categorize content based on your preferences.

European Economic Area (EEA) developers If your billing address is in the European Economic Area, effective on 8 July 2025, the Google Maps Platform EEA Terms of Service will apply to your use of the Services. Functionality varies by region. Learn more.

Geocoding translates an address into a location on a map. When you geocode an address, the response contains the:

  * Place ID of the location
  * Latitude and longitude coordinates of the location
  * Plus Code of the location
  * Expanded address details

## Geocode request

A geocode request is an HTTP GET request. You can specify the address as an unstructured string:
    
    https://geocode.googleapis.com/v4/geocode/address/`ADDRESS_STRING`

Or as a structured set of address components represented by query parameters:
    
    https://geocode.googleapis.com/v4/geocode/address?`STRUCTURED_ADDRESS`

You typically use the structured format when processing address components captured in an HTML form.

Pass all other parameters as URL parameters or, for parameters such as the API key and field mask, in headers as part of the GET request.

Note: URLs must be properly encoded to be valid and are limited to 4096 characters for all web services. Be aware of this limit when constructing your URLs. Note that different browsers, proxies, and servers may have different URL character limits as well.

### Pass an unstructured address string

An unstructured address is an address formatted as a string or a Plus Code. Address geocoding does not resolve latitude and longitude coordinates, or other unstructured strings that don't represent an address or a Plus Code. Requests using such strings are not supported and may lead to error responses or unspecified behavior. Examples of unsupported queries include the following:

Query type  | Example
--- | ---
Latitude and longitude coordinates. 
You can also make the request using a curl command:
    
    curl -H "X-Goog-Api-Key: `API_KEY`" \
    "https://geocode.googleapis.com/v4/geocode/address/1600+Amphitheatre+Parkway,+Mountain+View,+CA"

Addresses can contain many types of special characters. For example, a "/" as in "7/1 King St, Concord West". URL encode the "/" as `%2F`:
    
    https://geocode.googleapis.com/v4/geocode/address/7%2F1+King+St,+Concord+West
    ?key=`API_KEY`

Another common example is the "#" character, as in "9500 W Bryn Mawr Ave #650, Rosemont". URL encode the "#" as `%2FE`:
    
    https://geocode.googleapis.com/v4/geocode/address/9500+W+Bryn+Mawr+Ave+%23650,+Rosemont?key=`API_KEY`

In the next example, you specify an unstructured address string as the Plus Code `849VCWC8+R4`. Ensure that you URL-encode the "+" character as `%2B`:
    
    https://geocode.googleapis.com/v4/geocode/address/849VCWC8%2BR4?key=`API_KEY`
    

### Pass a structured address

Specify a structured address by using the `address` query parameter, of type `PostalAddress`. The `PostalAddress` object lets you specify some or all address components in the request as individual query parameters.

For example, to specify only the zip code of the address you use `PostalAddress.postalCode`:
    
    https://geocode.googleapis.com/v4/geocode/address?address.postalCode=01062&key=`API_KEY`
    

To specify multiple address components, such as for address components captured in an HTML form, use multiple query parameters:
    
    https://geocode.googleapis.com/v4/geocode/address?address.addressLines=1600+Amphithreater+Pkwy&address.locality=Mountain+View&address.administrativeArea=CA&key=`API_KEY`
    

### Use OAuth to make a request

Geocoding API v4 supports OAuth 2.0 for authentication. To use OAuth with the Geocoding API, the OAuth token must be assigned the correct scope. Geocoding API supports the following scopes for use with forward geocoding:

  * `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/maps-platform.geocode` — Use with all Geocoding API methods.
  * `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/maps-platform.geocode.address` — Use only with `GeocodeAddress` for forward geocoding.

Also, you can use the general `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform` scope for all Geocoding API methods. That scope is useful during development, but not production, because it is a general scope that allows access to all methods.

For more information and examples, see Use OAuth.

## Region biasing

In a geocoding request, you can instruct the Geocoding service to return results biased to a particular region by using the `regionCode` parameter. This parameter takes a two-character CLDR code value specifying the region bias. Most CLDR codes are identical to ISO 3166-1 codes.

There is no default value for `regionCode`. For example, a geocode for "Toledo" returns results for the US and for Spain:
    
    https://geocode.googleapis.com/v4/geocode/address/Toledo?key=`API_KEY`

#### Sampled path requests

  * `path` (required) defines a path on the earth for which to return elevation data. This parameter defines a set of two or more ordered {latitude,longitude} pairs defining a path along the surface of the earth. This parameter must be used in conjunction with the `samples` parameter described below. There is a 512 point limit for this specific parameter. For more information, see Specify Paths below.
  * `samples` (required) specifies the number of sample points along a path for which to return elevation data. The `samples` parameter divides the given `path` into an ordered set of equidistant points along the path.

### Specify locations

Positional requests are indicated through use of the `locations` parameter, indicating elevation requests for the specific locations passed as latitude/longitude values.

The `locations` parameter may take the following arguments:

  * A single coordinate: `locations=40.714728,-73.998672`

### Specify paths

Sampled path requests are indicated through use of the `path` and `samples` parameters, indicating a request for elevation data along a path at specified intervals. As with positional requests using the `locations` parameter, the `path` parameter specifies a set of latitude and longitude values. Unlike a positional request, however, the `path` specifies an ordered set of vertices. Rather than return elevation data only at the vertices, path requests are sampled along the length of the path, based on the number of `samples` specified (inclusive of the endpoints).

The `path` parameter may take either of the following arguments:

  * An array of two or more comma-separated coordinate text strings separated using the pipe ('`|`') character: `path=40.714728,-73.998672|-34.397,150.644`
  * Encoded coordinates using the Encoded Polyline Algorithm: `path=enc:gfo}EtohhUxD@bAxJmGF`

Latitude and longitude coordinate strings are defined using numerals within a comma-separated text string. For example, "40.714728,-73.998672|-34.397, 150.644" is a valid `path` value. Latitude and longitude values must correspond to a valid location on the face of the earth. Latitudes can take any value between `-90` and `90` while longitude values can take any value between `-180` and `180`. If you specify an invalid latitude or longitude value, your request will be rejected as a bad request.

You may pass up to 512 coordinates within an array or encoded polyline, while still constructing a valid URL. Note that when passing multiple coordinates, the accuracy of any returned data may be of lower resolution than when requesting data for a single coordinate. Exceeding 512 points or coordinates in the 'locations' or 'path' parameters returns an `INVALID_REQUEST` response.
